plan: Given the common knowledge of rationality and a single round, the optimal strategy is to bid slightly above the expected value of the second highest bid. Since values are between $0 and $49, the expected value of the highest of the other two bids is approximately (2/3) * 49 = $32.67. However, since we only have one round, and risk aversion is not explicitly modeled, a more conservative bid closer to my value is reasonable. I will bid $21.10 to increase my chances of winning without overpaying.

Given the common knowledge of rationality, the optimal bidding strategy converges to bidding your true value minus a small increment. This is because any bid above your value risks winning the auction at a loss. Bidding slightly below your value ensures you win only when the potential profit is positive. Since this is round 1, and there's no history, I'll bid slightly below my value of $22 to maximize potential profit while minimizing risk.

Given the common knowledge of rationality and a single round, the optimal strategy is to bid slightly above the expected value of the second-highest bid. Since values are uniformly distributed between $0 and $49, the expected value of the highest of the other two bids is (2/3) * 49 = 32.67. To maximize profit, bid slightly above this, but considering my own value of $13, I should bid conservatively. Bidding too high risks paying more than the item is worth to me.
